metadata.summary: This summary of the 2024 European Association of Urology guidelines addresses the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of urinary tract and male accessory-gland infections. It also covers infection control, antimicrobial stewardship, and antibiotic prophylaxis around urological procedures. Its recommendations are intended to support clinical decisions while allowing for individual patient circumstances and preferences.

target_population: Men with urinary tract or male accessory-gland infections

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not screen for or treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in women without risk factors, patients with well-regulated diabetes mellitus, postmenopausal women, elderly institutionalised patients, patients with a dysfunctional and/or reconstructed lower urinary tract, renal transplant recipients, patients awaiting arthroplasty, or patients with recurrent urinary tract infections.
prophylaxis.target_population: The specified groups with asymptomatic bacteriuria

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not screen for or treat asymptomatic bacteriuria before cardiovascular surgery.
Screen for and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria before a urological procedure that breaches the mucosa.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients awaiting a urological procedure that breaches the mucosa

prophylaxis.recommendation: Screen for and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria with a standard short-course regimen or single-dose fosfomycin trometamol. The guideline describes the supporting evidence as low quality and notes that a newer, methodologically stronger study found the benefit of antibiotics less evident.
prophylaxis.duration: Standard short course or single dose

prophylaxis.recommendation: Counsel patients on avoiding risk factors before progressing to non-antimicrobial measures and then antimicrobial prophylaxis.
Advise increased fluid intake, which might lower recurrence risk.
Use vaginal oestrogen replacement to prevent recurrence.
Use immunoactive prophylaxis to reduce recurrent UTI.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with recurrent UTI in all age groups

prophylaxis.recommendation: Advise patients about local or oral probiotic-containing strains with demonstrated efficacy for restoring vaginal flora.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients seeking prevention of recurrent UTI

prophylaxis.recommendation: Advise patients about cranberry products to reduce episodes, while explaining that the supporting evidence is low quality and contradictory.
Use D-mannose to reduce episodes, while informing patients that evidence of effectiveness is weak and contradictory overall.
Use methenamine hippurate to reduce recurrence.
prophylaxis.target_population: Women with recurrent UTI and no urinary tract abnormalities

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use endovesical hyaluronic acid instillations, alone or with chondroitin sulfate, after less invasive preventive approaches have failed. Explain that further studies must confirm the initial trial findings.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with recurrent UTI for whom less invasive prevention has been unsuccessful

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use continuous or postcoital antimicrobial prophylaxis when non-antimicrobial interventions have failed, and counsel patients about possible adverse effects.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with recurrent UTI after unsuccessful non-antimicrobial interventions

prophylaxis.recommendation: Keep catheterisation as short as possible and use hydrophilic coated catheters to reduce CA-UTI.
Do not generally treat catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria, but treat it before a traumatic urinary tract intervention, such as transurethral resection of the prostate.
Do not put topical antiseptics or antimicrobials on the catheter, urethra, or meatus, and do not give prophylactic antimicrobials to prevent CA-UTI.
Do not routinely give antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent clinical UTI after urethral catheter removal or during intermittent self-catheterisation.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients after urethral catheter removal or performing intermittent self-catheterisation

prophylaxis.recommendation: Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not recommended for urodynamics, cystoscopy, or extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy.
Give Trimethoprim prophylaxis.
Give a single dose of Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
Give a Cephalosporin group 2 or 3.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing TUR of the prostate

prophylaxis.recommendation: Give an Aminopenicillin plus a b-lactamase inhibitor only when postoperative sepsis risk is high.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing TUR of the bladder who have a high risk of postoperative sepsis

prophylaxis.recommendation: Options include prophylaxis targeted by rectal swab or stool culture; augmentation with two or more different antibiotic classes, which conflicts with antibiotic stewardship principles; or alternatives including Fosfomycin trometamol (eg, 3 g before and 3 g 24–48 h after biopsy), Cephalosporin (eg, ceftriaxone 1 g i.m.; cefixime 400 mg p.o. for 3 d starting 24 h before biopsy), or Aminoglycoside (eg, gentamicin 3mg/kg i.v.; amikacin 15mg/kg i.m.). Check local guidance for Fosfomycin trometamol because its prostate-biopsy indication was withdrawn in Germany after the manufacturers did not submit the required pharmacokinetic data.
prophylaxis.duration: The listed Fosfomycin trometamol example gives doses before and 24–48 h after biopsy; the cefixime example lasts 3 d starting 24 h before biopsy.

prophylaxis.recommendation: The panel could not recommend either for or against antibiotic prophylaxis because the scientific evidence was too weak.

infection_management.prevention: Restrict treatment to situations with demonstrated patient benefit to avoid selecting antimicrobial resistance and eliminating potentially protective colonisation.
infection_management.management: Persistent growth of urease-producing Proteus mirabilis requires exclusion of urinary tract stones.

For women with mild to moderate symptoms, symptomatic treatment such as ibuprofen may be considered instead of an antimicrobial after discussion with the patient. Select an antimicrobial according to pathogen susceptibility, clinical efficacy, tolerability, ecological effects, and cost or availability. If symptoms persist through treatment or resolve and recur within 2 wk, obtain a urine culture and susceptibility test; consider retreatment with a different agent for 7 d, assuming the original agent is ineffective against the organism. Routine post-treatment urine testing is not indicated when the patient is asymptomatic.

infection_management.prevention: Attempt risk-factor counselling, then non-antimicrobial measures, and then antimicrobial prophylaxis in that order.
infection_management.management: Confirm recurrent UTI by urine culture. Short-term self-administered antimicrobial therapy should be considered for patients with good compliance.

Obtain a urine culture and susceptibility test in every case and promptly distinguish possible obstruction by imaging. Oral empirical options are fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins; avoid nitrofurantoin, oral fosfomycin, and pivmecillinam because efficacy data are insufficient. Hospitalised patients should initially receive intravenous antimicrobials. Reserve carbapenems and novel broad-spectrum agents for early culture findings indicating multidrug-resistant organisms; optimise treatment after susceptibility results. Patients who improve and tolerate oral fluids may switch from parenteral to oral therapy. Short outpatient antibiotic courses have shown equivalent clinical and microbiological success to longer courses but higher recurrence within 4–6 wk, so their use must reflect local policy and resistance patterns.

Address the urological abnormality or underlying complicating factor. Obtain culture and susceptibility results to tailor initial empirical treatment, then use an appropriate agent for the isolated uropathogen. For infection with systemic symptoms, empirical options are Amoxicillin plus an aminoglycoside, a second-generation cephalosporin plus an aminoglycoside, or an intravenous third-generation cephalosporin. Use ciprofloxacin only if local resistance is <10% when treatment is entirely oral, hospitalisation is unnecessary, and the patient has anaphylaxis to b-lactam antimicrobials. Do not use ciprofloxacin or other fluoroquinolones empirically for patients from urology departments or those who used fluoroquinolones in the last 6 mo. Treatment generally lasts 7 d to 14 d, including 14 d for men when prostatitis cannot be excluded; relate duration closely to treatment of the underlying abnormality. A shorter course, eg, 7 d, may be considered when the patient is haemodynamically stable, has been afebrile for at least 48 h, and a short course is desirable because of relative contraindications to the antibiotic.

infection_management.prevention: Minimise catheterisation duration, use hydrophilic coated catheters, and avoid routine antimicrobial prophylaxis.
infection_management.management: Treat symptomatic CA-UTI according to complicated UTI recommendations. Obtain a urine culture before antimicrobials in catheterised patients whose catheter has been removed, and replace or remove an indwelling catheter before starting treatment. Cloudy or odorous urine alone does not distinguish CA-UTI from catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria. Pyuria does not establish CA-UTI or justify treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria; its absence in a symptomatic patient suggests another diagnosis.

Assess full SOFA or quick SOFA, collect urine and two sets of blood cultures before antimicrobials, and include drainage-fluid samples when applicable. Give high-dose broad-spectrum parenteral antimicrobials within the first hour after sepsis is clinically suspected, then adapt treatment to culture results. Provide immediate life support, investigate early with sonography or computed tomography, and control the source by removing foreign bodies, relieving obstruction, and draining urinary tract abscesses. Collaborative care involving urology, intensive care, and infectious disease specialists is recommended. The regimen table places 7–10 d beside Cefotaxime and notes that longer courses are appropriate for patients with a slow clinical response; Gentamicin and Amikacin have not been studied as monotherapy for urosepsis.

infection_management.prevention: Evaluate and treat sexual partners while protecting patient confidentiality.
infection_management.management: Start empirical treatment when severe urethritis is diagnosed; for mild symptoms, defer treatment until NAAT results guide selection. Use pathogen-directed therapy informed by local resistance data. Obtain a urethral swab culture before treatment when the gonorrhoea NAAT is positive to assess antimicrobial resistance.

Do not perform prostatic massage. Give high-dose parenteral bactericidal antimicrobials, such as broad-spectrum penicillins, a third-generation cephalosporin, or a fluoroquinolone; an aminoglycoside may be added initially. Once infection parameters normalise, switch to oral treatment to complete 2–4 wk. Urinary retention may be managed by urethral or suprapubic catheterisation; recent evidence suggests suprapubic catheterisation may reduce subsequent chronic bacterial prostatitis. Conservative treatment may work for a prostatic abscess <1 cm in diameter, whereas larger abscesses are better managed with single aspiration or continuous drainage.

Fluoroquinolones are recommended as first-line empirical treatment. The suggested course is 4–6 wk. Doxycycline is listed only for C. trachomatis or Mycoplasma infections, Azithromycin only for C. trachomatis, and Metronidazole only for T. vaginalis.

infection_management.prevention: For a proven sexually transmitted infection, report the infection, check cure, and trace and treat contacts.
infection_management.management: If torsion is suspected, perform urgent surgical exploration. When gonorrhoea is likely, use Ceftriaxone 1000 mg i.m. or i.v. plus a course of an antibiotic active against Chlamydia trachomatis. When gonorrhoea is unlikely, use one antibiotic or a combination of two active against Chlamydia trachomatis and Enterobacterales; consider parenteral treatment if infection is severe. If treatment fails or an abscess is present, perform scrotal ultrasound and clinical assessment.

Give a broad-spectrum antibiotic at presentation and refine treatment according to cultures and clinical response. Adequate repeated surgical debridement and urinary diversion by suprapubic catheter are necessary to reduce mortality. Do not use adjunctive treatments outside clinical trials.

infection_management.prevention: Discuss transmission, self-surveillance for new lesions, and the partial protection condoms provide against HPV.
infection_management.management: Options for lesions include patient-applied imiquimod 5%, sinecatechins 15% and 10%, or podophyllotoxin 0.5%, and clinician-administered cryotherapy or surgical treatment. Arrange follow-up when treatment is complete and again at 6 mo; switch treatment for recurrence.

Use combination drug treatment first line. For newly diagnosed disease, the cited World Health Organisation regimen lasts 6 mo: 2 mo of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by 4 mo of isoniazid and rifampicin. For MDR-TB resistant to rifampicin and isoniazid, use an individualised intensive-phase regimen with at least five effective TB medicines, including pyrazinamide and four core second-line medicines. Do not use thioacetazone in patients seropositive for human immunodeficiency virus. Evidence was insufficient for a definitive surgical recommendation; assess surgery individually according to disease location, progression, and genitourinary damage.

A systematic review and meta-analysis identified female sex, prolonged catheterisation, diabetes, and longer hospital or intensive care unit stays as risk factors.

conditions.name: Genitourinary tuberculosis
conditions.description: An extrapulmonary TB manifestation that may involve any genitourinary organ and is almost always secondary to haematogenous spread of chronic latent TB infection (LTBI). Risk factors include primary TB or LTBI, diabetes, older age, low body mass index, oncological comorbidities, immunosuppression including human immunodeficiency virus, renal failure, and poor socioeconomic conditions. No single test establishes the diagnosis.
conditions.epidemiology: GUTB accounted for 4.6% of extrapulmonary TB cases in the EU between 1997 and 2017. Estimated lifetime reactivation risk is up to 15%. More than 50% of patients may need ablative, endoscopic, or reconstructive surgery. Among GUTB cases, 26.9% have a nonfunctioning unilateral kidney and 7.4% have renal failure.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Possible nonspecific symptoms include haematuria, increased urinary frequency, difficulty voiding, and abdominal, lumbar, or suprapubic pain. Women may have menstrual irregularities or pelvic pain. Infertility may prompt presentation, although infertility and TB are not addressed in detail.

special_populations.considerations: A meta-analysis found benefit from treating asymptomatic bacteriuria during pregnancy, but most included studies had low methodological quality and the evidence for the recommendation is low quality. A newer, higher-quality study found less clear benefit. Pregnancy also calls for attention to possible complicating factors in pyelonephritis.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Screen for and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria with a standard short course or single-dose fosfomycin trometamol. For pyelonephritis, preferentially use ultrasound or MRI to investigate complicating factors without exposing the foetus to radiation. Outpatient parenteral antimicrobial treatment may be considered when symptoms are mild and close follow-up is feasible; more severe illness usually requires hospitalisation and supportive care. After clinical improvement, treatment may switch from parenteral to oral therapy for a total of 7–10 d.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Urological infections are common, have varied manifestations, and can substantially affect wellbeing and quality of life. The panel aimed to provide evidence-based guidance on diagnosing, treating, and preventing urinary tract infections (UTIs) and male accessory-gland infections, while addressing infection control and antimicrobial stewardship. For the 2024 guidelines, it identified and assessed new evidence through a structured literature review that searched Medline, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Libraries. Recommendations focused on clinically important decisions. Their strength reflected the balance of benefits and harms, evidence quality and certainty, and patient values and preferences. Principal messages include taking a thorough history and performing a physical examination, selecting antibiotic agents, doses, and durations according to current evidence, and using antimicrobial stewardship to address increasing resistance. The overview is intended to support clinical implementation, with particular attention to limiting antibiotic use in response to the global resistance threat.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: UTIs are among the most common bacterial infections, and multiple specialties participate in their diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. Presentations extend from relatively mild uncomplicated infection to complicated UTIs, pyelonephritis, and urosepsis. Severe UTIs have increased even as overall sepsis incidence has declined. Increasing antimicrobial resistance, particularly in complicated UTIs that include pyelonephritis, makes treatment more difficult. The European Association of Urology (EAU) panel prepared evidence-based guidance on UTIs and male accessory-gland infections and also addresses infection control and antimicrobial stewardship. Guidelines represent the best evidence available to the experts but do not guarantee the best outcome for every patient. They provide a framework rather than replacing clinical judgment: individual circumstances, values, and preferences remain relevant. The panel includes urologists, an infectious disease specialist, and a clinical microbiologist.

document_sections.heading: 2. Methods
document_sections.content: For the 2024 guidelines, the panel systematically identified, assembled, and assessed new evidence, searching Medline, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Libraries. It formulated recommendations around decisions important to clinical care. Recommendation strength reflected the relative desirable and undesirable effects of management options, evidence quality and certainty, and the character and variability of patient preferences. A recommendation is rated strong when evidence quality is high and/or benefits compare favourably with harms and patient preferences. A weak rating applies when evidence quality is lower and/or benefits and preferences are less certain.

document_sections.heading: 3.1. UTI classification
document_sections.content: UTIs form a heterogeneous spectrum, from mild to life-threatening illness, with corresponding differences in diagnosis and management; stratifying patients is therefore important. Several classification systems exist. They share the premise that complicated UTIs carry greater risks of recurrence, progression, chronicity, and severe outcomes than uncomplicated UTIs. Fig. 1 presents the uncomplicated-versus-complicated UTI concept and its associated presentations and risk categories.

document_sections.heading: 3.2. Asymptomatic bacteriuria in adults
document_sections.content: Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ABU) is frequent and represents commensal colonisation. Without urinary symptoms, its definition requires bacterial growth >105 cfu/ml in a midstream urine specimen from two consecutive samples in women or a single sample in men. The organisms resemble those found in uncomplicated or complicated UTIs according to the patient's risk factors. Cystoscopy and/or upper-tract imaging is not obligatory when the remaining history is unremarkable. Persistent isolation of the urease-producing organism Proteus mirabilis requires exclusion of urinary stones. Men should undergo digital rectal examination to assess for prostatic disease. Clinical studies indicate that ABU can protect against subsequent symptomatic infection. Treatment should consequently be limited to situations of demonstrated patient benefit, avoiding selection for antimicrobial resistance and elimination of a potentially protective strain. A meta-analysis found benefit from treating ABU during pregnancy, but most constituent studies had low methodological quality and dated from the 1960s to 1980s. Because diagnostic and treatment practices and access to care have since changed substantially, evidence quality for this recommendation is low; a newer, methodologically stronger study found less evident benefit from antibiotic treatment. Table 1 sets out the ABU screening and treatment recommendations and their Strong or Weak ratings, including groups in whom screening or treatment is discouraged and circumstances in which both are recommended.

document_sections.heading: 3.3. Uncomplicated cystitis
document_sections.content: Uncomplicated cystitis comprises acute, sporadic, or recurrent cystitis in nonpregnant women without relevant known urinary-tract anatomical or functional abnormalities or comorbidities. Risk factors include intercourse, spermicide use, a new sexual partner, maternal UTI history, and childhood UTI. Escherichia coli causes most cases. A focused history of dysuria, frequency, and urgency, together with absence of vaginal discharge, permits a high-probability diagnosis. Genitourinary symptoms in older women do not necessarily indicate cystitis. For typical symptoms, urine culture or dipstick testing adds little diagnostic accuracy, although a dipstick can help when the diagnosis is uncertain. Urine culture is recommended for suspected acute pyelonephritis, atypical symptoms, pregnancy, or symptoms that persist or return within 4 wk after treatment completion. Women with mild to moderate symptoms may consider symptomatic treatment, such as ibuprofen, instead of an antimicrobial after individual consultation. Antimicrobial selection should account for pathogen coverage and susceptibility, clinical efficacy for the indication, tolerability and adverse effects, ecological consequences, and cost or availability. Table 2 presents suggested antimicrobial regimens. Routine urinalysis or culture after treatment is not indicated in an asymptomatic patient. If symptoms persist to treatment completion or disappear and recur within 2 wk, obtain urine culture and susceptibility results. In that situation, assume the organism is not susceptible to the original agent and consider a different agent for a 7-d course.

document_sections.heading: 3.4. Recurrent UTIs
document_sections.content: Recurrent UTIs (rUTIs) are repeated uncomplicated and/or complicated infections occurring at least three UTIs/yr or two UTIs in the last 6 mo. They can involve the lower tract as cystitis or the upper tract as pyelonephritis; repeated pyelonephritis warrants consideration of a complicated cause. rUTIs diminish quality of life, including social and sexual relationships, self-esteem, and ability to work. Table 3 groups associated risk factors by age in women. Prevention comprises counselling about avoidable risk factors, non-antimicrobial interventions, and then antimicrobial prophylaxis, attempted in that order. Table 4 gives diagnostic and preventive recommendations with Strong or Weak ratings; it addresses urine-culture confirmation, when extensive investigation is unwarranted, fluid intake, vaginal oestrogen, immunoactive and other non-antimicrobial measures, and antimicrobial prophylaxis or patient-initiated treatment. It cautions that evidence for cranberry products is low and contradictory, evidence for D-mannose is weak and contradictory, and initial findings for endovesical instillations require further studies.

document_sections.heading: 3.5. Uncomplicated pyelonephritis
document_sections.content: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis is confined to nonpregnant, premenopausal women without known relevant urological abnormalities or comorbidities. Typical features are fever (>38 C), chills, flank pain, nausea, vomiting, or costovertebral-angle tenderness, with or without cystitis symptoms. Routine diagnostic testing should include urine white and red blood cells and nitrite; every case also requires urine culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Upper-tract ultrasound should exclude obstruction or renal stones in patients with previous urolithiasis, impaired renal function, or high urine pH. Consider contrast-enhanced computed tomography or excretory urography if fever persists after 72 h of treatment, or immediately upon clinical deterioration. In pregnancy, ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is preferred when investigating complicating factors to avoid fetal radiation exposure. Rapid imaging-based distinction from potentially obstructive pyelonephritis matters because obstruction can quickly lead to urosepsis. Only fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins can be recommended for empiric oral treatment. Oral cephalosporins produce significantly lower blood and urine concentrations than intravenous administration. Avoid nitrofurantoin, oral fosfomycin, and pivmecillinam because efficacy data are insufficient. A short outpatient antibiotic course has been shown to achieve clinical and microbiological success equivalent to longer courses, but carries more recurrence within 4–6 wk; local policy and resistance patterns should guide its use. Patients needing admission should initially receive intravenous treatment, such as a fluoroquinolone, an aminoglycoside with or without ampicillin, or an extended-spectrum cephalosporin or penicillin. Reserve carbapenems and novel broad-spectrum agents for early culture evidence of multidrug-resistant organisms; choose according to local resistance and refine using susceptibility findings. Signs of urosepsis warrant empiric coverage for extended-spectrum b-lactamase–producing organisms. Patients improving after parenteral treatment who can take oral fluids may change to oral therapy. Pregnant patients with mild symptoms may be managed as outpatients with suitable parenteral agents if close follow-up is feasible; more severe illness generally requires hospitalisation and supportive care. Following improvement, parenteral therapy may be changed to oral treatment for a total duration of 7–10 d. Men with febrile UTI, pyelonephritis, recurrent infection, or suspected complicating factors should receive at least 2 wk, preferably with a fluoroquinolone, because prostatic involvement is frequent. Tables 5 and 6 provide suggested empiric oral and parenteral regimens, respectively, with doses, durations where given, and qualifications.

document_sections.heading: 3.6. Complicated UTIs
document_sections.content: A complicated UTI (cUTI) occurs in a person whose host factors or urinary-tract anatomical or functional abnormalities are thought to impede eradication relative to an uncomplicated infection. Management must consider multidrug-resistant uropathogens. Table 7 lists commonly associated factors. Because cUTI covers many underlying conditions and patient groups, one uniform approach to investigation and treatment is inadequate, although general management principles apply. The recommendations in Table 8 draw on the Stichting Werkgroep Antibioticabeleid (SWAB) guidance of the Dutch Working Party on Antibiotic Policy and carry Strong ratings. Typical symptoms include dysuria, urgency, frequency, flank or suprapubic pain, costovertebral-angle tenderness, and fever, but presentation can be atypical with neuropathic bladder disturbance, catheter-associated UTI (CA-UTI), or prior radical cystectomy with urinary diversion. Illness can range from obstructive acute pyelonephritis threatening urosepsis to postoperative CA-UTI. Urine culture is recommended. Compared with uncomplicated UTI, the microbial range is wider and resistance is more likely; commonly cultured species are E. coli, Proteus spp., Klebsiella spp., Pseudomonas spp., Serratia spp., and Enterococcus spp. Addressing urinary abnormalities and underlying complicating factors is mandatory. Antimicrobial choice depends on presenting severity, local resistance, and host factors such as allergy. Obtain urine culture and susceptibility testing, then adapt initial empiric therapy and continue with an appropriate agent, orally when suitable, for the isolated organism. A duration of 7 d to 14 d is generally recommended, with 14 d for men when prostatitis cannot be excluded; duration should be closely tied to management of the underlying abnormality. If haemodynamically stable and afebrile for at least 48 h, a shorter course such as 7 d may be considered when relative contraindications to the administered antibiotic make this desirable. Table 8 also restricts empirical ciprofloxacin according to resistance and clinical circumstances, discourages empirical fluoroquinolones in specified patients, and requires management of complicating factors.

document_sections.heading: 3.7. Catheter-associated UTIs
document_sections.content: Catheter-associated (CA)-UTI is infection in someone currently catheterised or catheterised during the preceding 48 h. It is the foremost cause of secondary health care–associated bacteraemia. Approximately 20% of hospital-acquired bacteraemias originate in the urinary tract, with associated mortality of approximately 10%. Bacteriuria develops during indwelling catheterisation at 3–8% per day; catheterisation duration is the leading risk factor for CA-UTI. A systematic review and meta-analysis identified greater risk among women, people with prolonged catheterisation or diabetes, and those with longer hospital or intensive-care stays. Compatible new or worsening manifestations include fever, rigors, altered mental state, malaise, or lethargy without another cause; flank pain, costovertebral-angle tenderness, acute haematuria, or pelvic discomfort; and, after catheter removal, dysuria, urgency, frequency, or suprapubic pain or tenderness. Odour or cloudiness alone cannot distinguish CA-ABU from CA-UTI. The microbiological definition is growth >103 cfu/ml of one or more bacterial species in one catheter urine specimen, or in midstream urine after removal of a urethral, suprapubic, or condom catheter within the previous 48 h. Pyuria does not establish CA-UTI, and its presence, absence, or degree cannot distinguish CA-ABU from CA-UTI. Pyuria with CA-ABU does not itself justify antimicrobial treatment; its absence in a symptomatic person suggests a diagnosis other than CA-UTI. Table 9 presents Strong and Weak recommendations on treatment and prevention, including management according to complicated-UTI guidance, culture before treatment, catheter removal or replacement, minimising catheter duration, hydrophilic catheters, and restrictions on treatment or prophylactic antimicrobials.

document_sections.heading: 3.8. Urosepsis
document_sections.content: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by an abnormal host response to infection. An increase of 2 points in the Sequential (Sepsis-related) Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score can indicate organ dysfunction. The quick SOFA (qSOFA) score offers rapid identification using a respiratory rate of 22 breaths/min, altered mental status, or systolic blood pressure of 100 mm Hg. Assess either full SOFA or qSOFA for systemic manifestations of sepsis. Microbiological sampling should include urine, two sets of blood cultures, and drainage fluid when applicable. Investigate early with imaging, including sonography and computed tomography. Management requires immediate adequate life support, timely appropriate antimicrobial treatment, adjunctive measures, and treatment of urinary-tract abnormalities. Prompt source control includes relieving obstruction and draining substantial urinary abscesses. Coordinated care by urology, intensive-care, and infectious-disease specialists is recommended. Table 10 assigns Strong ratings to recommendations on qSOFA assessment, cultures before antimicrobials, high-dose parenteral broad-spectrum treatment within the first hour after sepsis is clinically suspected, culture-guided adaptation, source control, and life support. Table 11 lists suggested antimicrobial regimens and indicates 7–10 d, with longer courses appropriate when clinical response is slow; its aminoglycosides have not been studied as monotherapy in urosepsis.

document_sections.heading: 3.9. Urethritis
document_sections.content: Urethritis has infectious and noninfectious causes and should be distinguished from other lower-tract infections. Urethral infection is commonly sexually transmitted. Distinguish gonococcal urethritis (GU) from non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU). NGU is a nonspecific diagnosis with possible causes including Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum, and Trichomonas vaginalis. The causal contribution of Ureaplasma spp. is disputed; recent evidence suggests U. urealyticum, but not U. parvum, can cause NGU. Possible manifestations are mucopurulent or purulent discharge, dysuria, and urethral itching, although many infections cause no symptoms. Start empiric treatment at diagnosis for severe urethritis. With mild symptoms, delay treatment so nucleic acid amplification test results can guide selection. Assess and treat sexual partners at risk while protecting patient confidentiality. Table 12 sets out Strong diagnostic and treatment recommendations covering Gram staining, validated NAAT before empirical therapy, resistance assessment where gonorrhoea testing is positive, pathogen-directed treatment informed by local resistance, and partner treatment. Table 13 provides pathogen-specific and persistent-urethritis regimens and alternatives. Its note reports increasing evidence that intravenous ceftriaxone is safe and effective for gonorrhoeal infection and avoids the discomfort of intramuscular injection, despite the absence of randomised controlled trials.

document_sections.heading: 3.10. Bacterial prostatitis
document_sections.content: Prostatitis is diagnosed frequently, but bacterial infection is confirmed in fewer than 10% of cases. Enterobacterales predominate in acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP); chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP) involves a wider range, potentially including atypical organisms. Urologists are advised to use the National Institute of Diabetes, Digestive, and Kidney Diseases classification, which separates confirmed or suspected bacterial prostatitis from chronic pelvic pain syndrome. ABP typically starts suddenly with voiding symptoms and distressing, poorly localised pain, often accompanied by malaise and fever. CBP requires symptoms lasting at least 3 mo; pain may affect the perineum, scrotum, penis, or inner leg, alongside lower urinary tract symptoms. Table 14 gives Strong and Weak diagnostic recommendations, including avoidance of prostatic massage in ABP, microbiological evaluation and other tests according to presentation, and selective ultrasound to exclude abscess. High-dose parenteral bactericidal treatment is recommended for ABP, using a broad-spectrum penicillin, third-generation cephalosporin, or fluoroquinolone; an aminoglycoside may be combined with any of these initially. Once infection parameters normalise, oral treatment may replace parenteral therapy and continue to a total of 2–4 wk. Fluoroquinolones are recommended first-line for empiric CBP treatment because of favourable pharmacokinetics, generally good safety, and activity against Gram-negative organisms including Pseudomonas aeruginosa and C. trachomatis. Table 15 lists CBP regimens and pathogen-specific restrictions. Approximately 10% of men with ABP develop urinary retention, manageable with urethral or suprapubic catheterisation; recent evidence suggests the suprapubic route may lower subsequent CBP risk. Both drainage and conservative care appear feasible for prostatic abscess. Conservative treatment may work for a cavity <1 cm in diameter, whereas larger abscesses are better managed with single aspiration or continuous drainage.

document_sections.heading: 3.11. Acute infective epididymitis
document_sections.content: Epididymitis is common and may be acute, chronic, or recurrent. Acute disease presents with epididymal pain, swelling, and increased temperature, sometimes extending to the testis and scrotal skin. In up to 90% of cases, pathogens migrate from the urethra or bladder and can be identified through appropriate testing. Enterobacterales, C. trachomatis, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are the principal isolated organisms. Fig. 2 supplies the diagnostic and treatment decision pathway for adult men with acute scrotal pain and swelling: suspected torsion prompts urgent surgical exploration; suspected epididymitis prompts microbiological investigation and treatment according to the likelihood of gonorrhoea, with assessment for abscess or treatment failure and follow-up for proven sexually transmitted infection. It specifies ceftriaxone 1000 mg i.m. or i.v. plus an antibiotic active against Chlamydia trchomatics when gonorrhoea is likely; otherwise, it specifies treatment active against Chlamydia trachomatis and Enterobacterales, with parenteral treatment considered for severe infection. Despite a lack of randomised controlled trials, increasing evidence supports intravenous ceftriaxone as safe and effective for gonorrhoeal infections and less uncomfortable than intramuscular injection.

document_sections.heading: 3.12. Fournier’s gangrene
document_sections.content: Fournier’s gangrene is an aggressive, often fatal polymicrobial infection of soft tissue in the perineum, perianal area, and external genitalia. Painful scrotal or perineal swelling with sepsis is typical. Risk factors for occurrence and death include immunocompromise, most often related to diabetes or malnutrition, recent urethral or perineal surgery, and high body mass index. In up to 40% of cases onset is less obvious, and unrecognised pain commonly delays treatment. Maintain high suspicion and examine carefully, particularly in patients with obesity. Computed tomography or MRI can delineate pararectal involvement and indicate a possible need for bowel diversion. Give a broad-spectrum antibiotic at presentation and subsequently adjust it to cultures and clinical response; Table 16 lists suggested regimens for mixed microbiological causes. Internal necrosis generally extends considerably further than external findings imply. Adequate, repeated surgical debridement and urinary diversion through a suprapubic catheter are therefore necessary to lower mortality. Do not use adjunctive treatments outside clinical trials.

document_sections.heading: 3.13. Management of human papillomavirus in men
document_sections.content: Human papillomavirus is among the most frequently sexually transmitted viruses and includes oncogenic low- and high-risk variants as well as non-oncogenic viruses. Fig. 3 presents diagnosis, lesion treatment, and follow-up. Its pathway uses physical examination to identify lesions, allows magnification, and includes inspection of the urethral meatus. When examination does not settle the diagnosis, it includes an acetic acid test for subclinical lesions, biopsy for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected precancer or cancer, and possible dermatology consultation. Patient-applied lesion treatments shown are imiquimod 5%, sinecatechins 15% and 10%, and podophyllotoxin 0.5%; clinician-administered options include cryotherapy and surgical approaches. It shows follow-up after completion of treatment and again at 6 mo, treatment change for recurrence, and discussion of natural history, transmission, self-surveillance, and the partial protection condoms provide. Further information is available in the full guideline.

document_sections.heading: 3.14. Genitourinary tuberculosis
document_sections.content: Tuberculosis (TB) is common worldwide, but its extrapulmonary form, genitourinary TB (GUTB), is often underestimated by urologists, especially in non-endemic areas such as Europe. GUTB accounted for 4.6% of extrapulmonary TB cases in the EU between 1997 and 2017. It can involve any genitourinary organ and is almost always secondary to bloodstream spread of chronic latent TB infection (LTBI). Risk factors include primary TB or LTBI, diabetes, older age, low body mass index, cancer-related comorbidity, immunosuppression including human immunodeficiency virus, renal failure, and socioeconomic disadvantage. Estimated lifetime reactivation risk is up to 15%. No single test establishes GUTB: diagnosis requires clinical suspicion grounded in history and supported by microbiology, molecular and histological testing, and imaging. Symptoms are commonly nonspecific, including haematuria, increased urinary frequency, difficulty voiding, and abdominal, lumbar, or suprapubic pain. Women may also have menstrual irregularity or pelvic pain. Infertility may lead patients to present, but infertility and TB are not considered in detail. Table 17 presents Strong and Weak diagnostic recommendations. Combination drug treatment is first-line. For newly diagnosed extrapulmonary TB, the World Health Organisation advises daily treatment for 6 mo: an initial 2 mo with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, then 4 mo with isoniazid and rifampicin. Multidrug-resistant TB, defined here by resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid, calls for individualised treatment with at least five effective TB drugs during the intensive phase, including pyrazinamide and four core second-line drugs. Table 18 details treatment regimens, doses, drug groups, and selection restrictions. More than 50% of patients may need ablative, endoscopic, or reconstructive surgery because infection can be destructive and diagnosis delayed. In one cited source, 26.9% of GUTB cases had a nonfunctioning unilateral kidney and 7.4% had renal failure. High-quality evidence on surgery is scarce, so the panel could not make a definitive recommendation for surgical intervention. Assess each patient individually and base the decision to operate on disease location, progression, extent, and genitourinary damage.

document_sections.heading: 3.15. Periprocedural antibiotic prophylaxis
document_sections.content: Urological surgeons should maintain asepsis to minimise infection from patients' own microbiota and from health care–associated sources. Measures include suitable instrument cleaning and sterilisation, regular thorough cleaning of operating and recovery areas, and careful disinfection of contamination sources. They should know procedure-specific local pathogen prevalence, susceptibility, and virulence so written local guidance can be established. Available evidence allowed the panel to formulate prophylaxis recommendations for urodynamics, cystoscopy, extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy, ureteroscopy, percutaneous nephrolithotomy, transurethral resection of the prostate, and transurethral resection of the bladder. Evidence for nephrectomy and prostatectomy was too weak for a recommendation either for or against prophylactic antibiotics. Table 19 lists the procedure-specific prophylaxis decisions and suggested agents. Its notes caution that augmented prophylaxis using two or more antibiotic classes conflicts with antimicrobial stewardship principles. They also report that the prostate-biopsy indication for fosfomycin trometamol was withdrawn in Germany because manufacturers did not provide the necessary supporting pharmacokinetic data; urologists are advised to check local guidance on its use for that procedure.

document_sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
document_sections.content: This summary presents current guidance on diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of urological infections to help clinicians put recommendations into practice. It particularly emphasises antimicrobial stewardship in response to the growing worldwide threat of antimicrobial resistance. A full guideline is available online.
